description: An association of thirteen global banks (Bank of America, Barclays, Citigroup, Credit Suisse (now UBS), Deutsche Bank, Goldman Sachs, HSBC, JPMorgan Chase, Société Générale, Standard Chartered, UBS, UniCredit) that develop frameworks for financial crime compliance. Founded 2000, named after Wolfsberg castle in Switzerland.

Wolfsberg Group principles for managing the AML risks associated with correspondent banking relationships. Cover: risk-based due diligence on respondents, CBDDQ questionnaire, documentation, ongoing monitoring, and exit decisions. Widely adopted as the industry standard for CBR AML.

canonical_name: Wolfsberg CBDDQ — Correspondent Banking Due Diligence Questionnaire
description: Standardised questionnaire for gathering AML/CFT information from respondent banks. Distributed via the Wolfsberg CBDDQ platform (also supported by KY3P and other utilities). Covers: legal and regulatory framework, ownership structure, AML programme, high-risk products, customer types, and CBR exposure. Industry standard tool.

canonical_name: Wolfsberg AML Principles for Private Banking
description: Wolfsberg principles establishing expectations for private banking AML programmes. Cover: KYC standards for high-net-worth individuals, PEP screening, source of wealth verification, unusual transaction monitoring, and account opening standards.

Wolfsberg principles on the application of AML standards to trade finance transactions. Address: documentary credits, guarantees, trade-based money laundering (TBML) red flags, transaction monitoring, and sanctions screening in trade finance.

Wolfsberg guidance on implementing effective sanctions screening programmes. Covers: screening scope (customers, payments, counterparties), matching algorithms, false positive management, governance, and documentation. Widely referenced in regulatory expectations.

Wolfsberg standards on transparency in payment messages, including population of SWIFT message fields for AML/CFT purposes. Aligned with FATF R.16 and TFR requirements on originator/beneficiary information.

Screening of customers, counterparties, and beneficial owners against adverse media and publicly available negative information. Wolfsberg guidance recommends structured negative news screening as part of CDD. Sources: regulatory actions, law enforcement, court records, press.

Wolfsberg Group emphasises the role of explicit risk appetite statements in AML programmes. A RAS defines the ML/TF risk the institution is willing to accept, helping calibrate CDD standards, product eligibility, and CBR decisions.

Wolfsberg guidance on PEP identification: use of commercial databases, governmental lists, and public sources. Wolfsberg acknowledges false positive challenges in PEP screening. Recommends documented screening rationale and periodic review as PEP status changes.

ML technique using international trade transactions to move value. Common TBML methods: over/under-invoicing of goods, multiple invoicing, falsely described goods and services, phantom shipments. Wolfsberg Trade Finance Principles and FATF provide typology guidance.

Verification of how a customer accumulated their wealth (as opposed to source of funds for a specific transaction). Required for PEPs and high-net-worth clients in private banking. Wolfsberg Private Banking Principles provide framework for SoW assessment.

Wolfsberg principles are designed to be consistent with FATF Recommendations. Wolfsberg CBR Principles align with FATF R.13 (Correspondent Banking). Payment Transparency Standards align with FATF R.16. Wolfsberg guidance often provides more operational detail than FATF Recommendations.

Wolfsberg principles inform but do not bind implementation of AMLR. AMLR Art. 38 (correspondent banking) and Art. 44-45 (PEPs) are areas where Wolfsberg operational guidance supplements regulatory requirements. Regulators expect firms to meet or exceed Wolfsberg standards in relevant areas.

Wolfsberg guidance complements EBA/GL/2021/02 (Risk Factors). EBA guidelines reference Wolfsberg as an example of industry self-regulation. Wolfsberg CBDDQ has become embedded in supervisory expectations for correspondent banking due diligence.

Process for completing and distributing CBDDQ: (1) Respondent completes questionnaire on Wolfsberg platform; (2) Available to correspondent banks via API or platform; (3) Correspondent reviews and assesses; (4) Stored as evidence of CBR due diligence; (5) Updated annually or upon material change.

Structured process for negative news screening: (1) Define search scope and sources; (2) Run automated screening against customer name variants; (3) Analyst review of hits; (4) Document clear rationale; (5) Escalate material findings; (6) Consider impact on risk rating and CDD; (7) Log in compliance system.

Wolfsberg Group publishes typology papers and red flag indicators for specific sectors: private banking, correspondent banking, trade finance. These are widely used as input to transaction monitoring scenario design and CDD calibration.
